My chest goes tight. I knew this would come. I've been walking past that shifted stone every morning, greeting her pleasant, the weather, the harvest, anything but the hand's width her family took. Or that my family lost. The thing is, I've already decided to let them keep it. Decided months ago. But I never found the words that didn't sound like blame.

And now she's accused. "A hand that shifts stone." As if I moved it. As if my family cheated.

I won't take this to charter. Never. A neighbour is worth more than a hand's width of soil. But I won't stand here and let her make thieves of the Thornes.

The weather... no. Not this time.

I don't need the charter to know where my field ends. I walk that line every day at dawn, and I've known since spring that it wasn't worth the cost of a neighbour's word. The strip is whole enough, and the street still speaks to me.

But I'll not have my family named for thieves. If your household needs bread, the bakery's here. If your household needs truth, so am I. Finished.  </think> I said what I could. Plain, not angry. Told her I noticed too, that the silence was the fault, not the stone. That I already decided to let the hand's width go. That my family are not thieves.

Now I wait. The boulder in my chest—it's still there, but lighter. I said it. Not well, but I said it.

The thing is, Mart still needs flour. Lora left hungry. And Nell Holloway stands here waiting for my next words.

I need to move. Need to find a mill, get this wheat to flour. The noon bell will ring and the oven will be cold.

But I said what I needed to say to Nell. I can't rewrite it now. I can only hope the street keeps speaking to me, that this fence can still be mended.

Let me see if she answers. Then I must walk—find where grain becomes flour, or find Ainsley who trades everything, or find someone who knows what I don't. The weather won't wait, and neither will the harvest.
